positions/reformed-spiritual-presence/on: In the Supper believers truly feed on the body and blood of Christ, not because Christ descends into the bread but because the Holy Spirit lifts them by faith into communion with the ascended Christ.
positions/reformed-spiritual-presence/co: The bread and wine remain bread and wine and are signs and seals of Christ’s body and blood.
Christ’s human body is locally in heaven; it is not enclosed in the elements.
By the secret power of the Spirit, believers really partake of Christ’s whole person, being nourished by his flesh and blood.
Unbelievers receive only the signs, to their judgement, not the reality.
The Supper strengthens union with Christ and with one another.
positions/reformed-spiritual-presence/or: Martin Bucer at Strasbourg, then John Calvin (Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper, 1541; Institutes 4.17, 1559), mediated between Luther and Zwingli. The Consensus Tigurinus (1549) united Calvin with Bullinger; the Belgic Confession (1561), Heidelberg Catechism (1563), Second Helvetic Confession (1566), Westminster Confession (1647) and, in substance, the Anglican Articles (XXVIII) teach it.
positions/reformed-spiritual-presence/st: It affirms a true feeding on Christ while honouring the reality of his ascended human body (Acts 3:21; Heb 8:1).
It gives the Holy Spirit a central role in uniting believers to Christ, consistent with the Bible’s teaching on union with Christ.
It has strong patristic resonance with the liturgical call "Lift up your hearts" (sursum corda) and Augustine’s distinction of sign and reality.
Lutherans charge that it makes the presence depend on faith, so that Christ’s word "this is my body" is not strictly true of the bread.
Catholics and Orthodox argue it is still a form of spiritualising that departs from the patristic language of change.
Zwinglians and many evangelicals find the language of "feeding on Christ’s flesh" obscure and hard to distinguish from their own spiritual communion.
positions/reformed-spiritual-presence/re: Calvinists reply that the Spirit "truly unites things separated by space" (Institutes 4.17.10), so the presence is real, not imaginary, though not local.
They argue that their view, not Zwingli’s, became the confessional Reformed position, and that the reality is objectively offered to all though received only by faith.
positions/reformed-spiritual-presence/co: Became the official teaching of Reformed, Presbyterian and (in substance) Anglican confessions.
Allowed Reformed–Lutheran rapprochement in the 20th century (Arnoldshain Theses 1957; Leuenberg 1973).
Often eroded in popular practice towards a memorial view, prompting revival movements (Mercersburg theology, 1840s).
positions/zwinglian-memorial/oneLine: The Lord’s Supper is a commemoration of Christ’s death and a public pledge of faith in which bread and wine signify, but do not contain, Christ’s body and blood.
positions/zwinglian-memorial/coreClaims/: In "this is my body" the word "is" means "signifies", as in "I am the vine" or "that rock was Christ".
Christ’s risen body is at the right hand of God and cannot be physically present in many places.
"It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing" (John 6:63): eating Christ means believing in him.
The Supper is a thankful remembrance (eucharistia) and the community’s oath of allegiance (sacramentum as soldier’s oath).
Christ is present to the faith of the gathered believers, not in the elements.
positions/zwinglian-memorial/keyTexts/0: Luke 22:19 ("this do in remembrance of me")
positions/zwinglian-memorial/origin: The Dutch lawyer Cornelius Hoen’s letter (c.1521) proposed that "is" means "signifies"; Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich adopted and developed this (letter to Matthew Alber, 1524; Commentary on True and False Religion, 1525). Zurich celebrated a simple memorial Supper from Easter 1525. Anabaptists (Schleitheim, 1527) and later Baptists and most evangelicals took up a memorial view. Zwingli’s own later writings (Fidei Ratio 1530; Fidei Expositio 1531) speak of a presence "by the contemplation of faith", richer than "mere memorialism".
positions/zwinglian-memorial/proponentsO: Many Baptist, Brethren, evangelical and Pentecostal churches
positions/zwinglian-memorial/strongestAr: Scripture regularly uses "is" figuratively, and the disciples could hardly have thought the bread in Jesus’ living hand was his body.
The command is "this do in remembrance of me", and Paul says we "proclaim the Lord’s death" in eating (1 Cor 11:26).
It safeguards the uniqueness of Christ’s finished sacrifice and his true, located humanity.
It removes superstition and clerical power over grace.
positions/zwinglian-memorial/strongestOb: Lutherans, Catholics and Orthodox argue it contradicts the plain sense of the words and the unanimous realism of the early Church (Ignatius, Justin).
Paul’s warnings about "not discerning the Lord’s body" and sickness and death among unworthy communicants (1 Cor 11:29–30) suggest more than a memorial.
Calvin and the Reformed argue it reduces the Supper to the believer’s act, rather than God’s gift.
positions/zwinglian-memorial/responses/0: Memorialists reply that "discerning the body" may refer to the Church as the body (1 Cor 10:17; 12:27), whose divisions Paul was rebuking.
positions/zwinglian-memorial/responses/1: They argue that patristic realism is often symbolic in its own idiom (Augustine, Tertullian’s "figure of my body", Against Marcion 4.40).
positions/zwinglian-memorial/consequence: Caused the rupture at Marburg (1529) and shaped Swiss, Anabaptist and Baptist worship.
Became the majority practical view among evangelical, Baptist and Pentecostal Christians worldwide.
Encouraged infrequent communion in some traditions (quarterly or monthly), though others celebrate weekly (Churches of Christ, Brethren).
positions/apostolic-succession/oneLine: Bishops, ordained by the laying on of hands in an unbroken line from the apostles, are the guardians of apostolic faith and the ministers through whom valid ordination and sacraments are transmitted.
positions/apostolic-succession/coreClaim: Christ commissioned the apostles, who appointed successors (Acts 14:23; 2 Tim 2:2; Titus 1:5).
An unbroken succession of bishops by ordination preserves the Church’s continuity and apostolic teaching.
Valid priesthood and (for most holders) valid Eucharist depend on ordination by bishops in succession.
The bishop is the focus of the local church’s unity (Ignatius).
For Catholics, the college of bishops is in communion with and under the bishop of Rome as Peter’s successor.
positions/apostolic-succession/origin: Attested in 1 Clement (c.96) and developed by Hegesippus and Irenaeus (c.180) as a public succession of teachers guaranteeing apostolic tradition against Gnostics; under Cyprian (c.250) it became the basis of sacramental validity. Universal in Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and East Syriac churches; retained by the Church of England (though Leo XIII’s Apostolicae Curae, 1896, declared Anglican orders "absolutely null and utterly void"), Old Catholics and the Church of Sweden; shared with Nordic and Baltic Lutherans by the Porvoo Agreement (1992).
positions/apostolic-succession/proponent: John Henry Newman and the Oxford Movement
positions/apostolic-succession/strongest: It is among the earliest documented structures of the post-apostolic Church and was universal by the end of the 2nd century, East and West.
It provides a visible, verifiable link to the apostles that guards against innovation and schism.
It explains how the Church preserved the canon and the creeds through bishops in council.

Protestants argue the New Testament uses "bishop" and "elder" interchangeably (Titus 1:5–7; Acts 20:17, 28) and that monepiscopacy developed later; apostolic succession is properly succession of doctrine.
Historians note gaps and uncertainties in early succession lists (e.g. the order of the first Roman bishops).
Critics argue it can make grace dependent on institutional pedigree; corrupt bishops have stood in succession while teaching error.
Churches without historic episcopate (Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal) display evident spiritual fruit and orthodoxy.
positions/apostolic-succession/responses: Defenders reply that monepiscopacy is clear by Ignatius (c.107) and that an orderly ministry derived from the apostles is implicit in the Pastoral Epistles.
Many (e.g. Anglicans, BEM 1982) present the historic episcopate as a sign of continuity rather than a guarantee, recognising the apostolicity of churches without it.
positions/apostolic-succession/consequen: Became the structural backbone of Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches.
Central to ecumenical disputes over the validity of orders (Apostolicae Curae 1896) and to ecumenical agreements (Porvoo 1992; Called to Common Mission 1999).
Shaped Protestant alternatives: presbyterian and congregational polities, and modern apostolic networks claiming charismatic rather than tactile succession.
positions/episcopal-polity/oneLine: The Church is governed by bishops, assisted by priests (presbyters) and deacons, with authority flowing through the episcopate rather than from congregations.
positions/episcopal-polity/coreClaims/0: There are three orders of ordained ministry: bishop, priest/presbyter and deacon.
positions/episcopal-polity/coreClaims/1: Bishops ordain, confirm, oversee dioceses and teach authoritatively.
positions/episcopal-polity/coreClaims/2: Bishops govern collegially in synods and councils (and, for Catholics, under the pope; for Orthodox, as autocephalous churches with patriarchs and synods).
positions/episcopal-polity/coreClaims/3: Laity participate through various councils but do not hold the power of orders.
positions/episcopal-polity/origin: The threefold ministry with one bishop per city is clear in Ignatius of Antioch (c.107) and universal by c.200. Methodists retained bishops in America (Coke and Asbury, 1784) without claiming tactile succession; some Lutheran churches retained bishops as a matter of good order.
positions/episcopal-polity/strongestArgu: It is the most ancient and widespread form of church order, attested within a generation of the apostles.
It provides clear oversight and unity across congregations and regions.
It mirrors the apostolic oversight of churches by figures such as Timothy and Titus.
positions/episcopal-polity/strongestObje: Presbyterians argue that New Testament "bishops" were the same as elders and that a single ruling bishop is a later development.
Congregationalists object that it concentrates power and weakens the priesthood of all believers.
Historically associated with state establishment and political power (prince-bishops, House of Lords).
positions/episcopal-polity/responses/0: Episcopalians, from Hooker on, argue that even if the threefold order developed, it did so under apostolic guidance and Spirit-led tradition.
positions/episcopal-polity/responses/1: Synodical government (e.g. Anglican houses of clergy and laity) balances episcopal authority with lay participation.
positions/episcopal-polity/consequences/: The polity of the large majority of the world’s Christians.
Conflict over bishops helped cause the English Civil Wars (Bishops’ Wars, 1639–40).
Methodist episcopacy shaped American denominational organisation.
positions/presbyterian-polity/oneLine: The Church is governed by elders (teaching and ruling) of equal rank, meeting in a hierarchy of representative courts: session, presbytery, synod and general assembly.
positions/presbyterian-polity/coreClaims: "Bishop" (overseer) and "elder" (presbyter) are the same office in the New Testament.
Each congregation is ruled by a session of elders, including lay ruling elders and ordained ministers.
Congregations are bound together by higher courts (presbyteries and assemblies) with real authority, as in the Jerusalem council (Acts 15).
Christ alone is head of the Church; no individual bishop or civil ruler governs it.
positions/presbyterian-polity/keyTexts/1: 1 Timothy 4:14 (laying on of hands by the presbytery); 5:17
positions/presbyterian-polity/origin: John Calvin’s Ecclesiastical Ordinances (Geneva, 1541) set out four offices (pastors, doctors, elders, deacons) and a consistory; the French Reformed national synod (1559), John Knox’s First Book of Discipline (1560) and Andrew Melville’s Second Book of Discipline (1578) developed graded courts; the Westminster Assembly’s Form of Presbyterial Church-Government (1645) became the model for Presbyterians worldwide, including the large Korean, Ghanaian and Brazilian Presbyterian churches.
positions/presbyterian-polity/strongestA: It matches the New Testament interchangeability of "bishop" and "elder" and the plurality of elders in each church.
Graded courts reflect the Jerusalem council’s binding decision for many churches (Acts 15:28; 16:4).
It balances clerical and lay leadership and provides accountability without a single ruler.
positions/presbyterian-polity/strongestO: Episcopalians argue it breaks continuity with the universal ancient Church order and with apostolic succession.
Congregationalists argue higher courts have no clear biblical warrant to override local congregations.
Critics note its record of division: Scottish and American Presbyterianism repeatedly split (Disruption of 1843; numerous American divisions).
positions/presbyterian-polity/responses/: Presbyterians reply that Jerome himself noted that bishops and presbyters were originally the same (Letter 146).
They argue that divisions arose from doctrinal conflicts that any polity would face, and that presbyterian courts provide a procedure for resolving them.
positions/presbyterian-polity/consequenc: Shaped the Scottish Reformation, the Puritan movement and the American Revolution era (representative government analogies).
Spread through missions to Korea (where Presbyterians number in the millions), Ghana, Cameroon, Brazil, Taiwan and elsewhere.
